The Big-scale sand smelt Atherina boyeri is a common coastal species in the Mediterranean basin, and field surveys indicate that individuals typically attain a maximum recorded total length of 20 centimeters [Li = 20 centimeters]. This ultimate size is relatively modest compared to other atherinids, reflecting its adaptation to shallow lagoon environments where food resources can be seasonally variable. Reproductive maturity, however, is achieved much earlier, at a total length of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a strategy that allows the species to exploit brief windows of favorable conditions in its variable habitat, ensuring that at least a portion of the cohort can reproduce even in years when growth is suppressed by low temperatures or scarce prey. The rapid progression from a larval mass of just 0.0028 grams [Wwb = 0.0028 grams] at the moment of yolk-sac resorption to the size at which gonadal development begins is a key feature of its life history, driven by high metabolic rates during the warm summer months.

Reproductive output in Atherina boyeri has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], reflecting the thermal regime typical of its spring spawning season. At this temperature, adult females produce approximately 27.9 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 27.9 eggs per spawning event] and spawn once per day [F_R_i = spawn once per day], a high fecundity that integrates both the size of individual clutches and the frequency of spawning events. This elevated reproductive output is a common trait among small, short-lived teleosts that rely on numerical output to offset elevated rates of larval mortality in the plankton. The eggs themselves are relatively small, with a diameter near 1.75 millimeters, and the corresponding wet weight at birth, representing the mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva, has been estimated at 0.0028 grams [Wwb = 0.0028 grams]. This initial mass imposes a tight constraint on the duration of the endotrophic phase, as the larva must locate suitable prey within a few days of hatching.

The species exhibits a pronounced shift in body mass as it progresses from the juvenile to the adult stage. Individuals at the onset of puberty have a wet weight of approximately 0.79 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.79 grams], which is dramatically less than the ultimate wet weight of 55.4 grams [Wwi = 55.4 grams] recorded for fully grown adults. This more than fifty-fold increase in mass between sexual maturation and the attainment of asymptotic size underscores the extended period of somatic investment that occurs concurrently with early reproductive activity. Field growth studies suggest that the relationship between length and mass in this species follows a strong allometric pattern, with the ultimate wet weight derived from a length-weight regression applied to the maximum recorded total length. The substantial post-puberty growth observed in Atherina boyeri is likely an adaptation to variable resource availability, allowing individuals to continue accumulating reserves even after they have begun contributing to the next generation.

Longevity in Atherina boyeri is limited, with a maximum lifespan of 4 years [am = 4 years] documented in wild populations maintained at an average water temperature of 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C]. This relatively short lifespan aligns with its early maturation and high reproductive output, placing the species firmly in the r-selected portion of the life-history continuum. The age-related mortality schedule is steep, with very few individuals surviving beyond their third spawning season, a pattern that has been corroborated by otolith-based age readings from multiple Mediterranean lagoons. This brief life span means that the population is highly dependent on consistent annual recruitment to maintain its numbers, making it vulnerable to consecutive years of poor spawning conditions or elevated egg and larval predation. Senescence-related physiological deterioration likely accelerates after the second year of life, contributing to the sharp decline in abundance among older age classes.

The morphological transformation from the pelagic larval stage to the benthic juvenile form is a critical bottleneck in the life cycle of Atherina boyeri. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, initially weighing just 0.0028 grams [Wwb = 0.0028 grams], rely entirely on endogenous yolk reserves until the mouth opens and the exotrophic transition is completed. The small mass constrains the duration of the endotrophic phase to only a few days at 18.3 °C [T = 18.3 °C], after which the larva must successfully initiate exogenous feeding. Following settlement, the juvenile fish grow rapidly, and the wet weight associated with the onset of puberty, 0.79 grams [Wwp = 0.79 grams], is typically reached within the first year of life. This rapid juvenile growth is supported by a diet of zooplankton and small benthic invertebrates, enabling the species to capitalize on the warm summer growing season before the onset of winter metabolic constraints.
